extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of Plato / classical political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Expository dialogue (Plato's Republic, Book II) exploring the nature and origin of justice, hypothetical city-building as method, and the character/education required of guardians. The text uses thought experiments (Gyges' ring, perfectly just/unjust lives) to probe moral psychology and political organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and nature of justice (social compromise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is described as a mean or compromise between the best (doing injustice with impunity) and the worst (suffering injustice without retaliation); laws and covenants arise because men cannot avoid both doing and suffering injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice is not presented as intrinsically advantageous at first glance, but as a mutual agreement born of necessity — honoured because individuals lack the power to be unjust without consequence. This framing is used as the initial account to be tested and refined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gyges ring thought-experiment (power reveals true motive)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person could act invisibly and with impunity (as with Gyges' ring), no one would be imagined to remain just; both the just and unjust would act identically when freed from consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an argument about human nature: that justice is practiced from fear of punishment/reputation rather than intrinsic desire. Serves as a test-case to challenge the intrinsic value of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance vs reality in moral action (reputation-driven justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: People commonly practice justice for appearances, honours, and the tangible benefits that reputation brings, rather than for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets, parents, and traditional education are criticized for teaching justice in terms of its rewards (praise, riches, divine favor), which makes appearance tyrannize over truth. The dialogue demands demonstration of justice's value independent of reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: proceed from larger (city) to smaller (individual)
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand justice in the individual, first examine justice as it appears in the State — the larger unit makes the quantity of justice more discernible and easier to analyze.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates proposes constructing an ideal city in speech as a methodological device: inspect the political/community level first, then map findings onto the individual soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: State arises from human needs and exchange (division of labor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A State originates because no one is self-sufficient; people specialize (husbandman, builder, weaver, shoemaker, etc.) and exchange their products, forming a community to satisfy mutual needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization is defended as producing more plentiful, easier, and better-quality goods: one person one craft, practiced at the right time, yields superior results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic institutions necessary to a State (market, money, merchants, retailers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A functioning city requires marketplaces, money-tokens for exchange, retailers (who stay in the market), merchants (who travel and trade), and various classes (hirelings) to fulfill roles not suited to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These institutional elements are presented as pragmatic requirements for exchange and for the city to meet its inhabitants' needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Healthy vs luxurious State distinction (necessities vs excess)
rubrics_metrics.description: A basic, healthy State provides necessities (food, shelter, clothing). A luxurious State introduces non-essential arts and desires (embroidery, painters, cooks, courtesans), which enlarge needs, require more territory/resources, and lead to conflict/war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis links excessive luxury to expansionist pressures and thus to the origin of many public evils, framing austerity as politically stabilizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: War and defence as specialized arts requiring full-time attention
rubrics_metrics.description: War is an art requiring as much time and specialization as other crafts; a soldier cannot be expected to be excellent if he simultaneously pursues other trades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore a city must select and train individuals exclusively for the guardianship/warrior role; tools and occasional practice are insufficient without lifelong devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and training of guardians (natural aptitude + education)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians should be selected for natural aptitude (physical and mental), then given prolonged training: they must be quick, swift, strong, brave, and possess spirit for fighting and defending the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is difficult and must aim to match nature to task; guardians require both inborn qualities and intensive cultivation of skill and courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral temper of guardians: dangerous to enemies, gentle to friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must combine high spirit (thumos) and courage with gentleness toward friends — avoiding internal savagery that would make them destructive within the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates highlights the tension between spiritedness and gentleness as a practical problem: training must channel aggressive capacities outward rather than inward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought-experiment for testing moral theories (perfectly just vs perfectly unjust lives)
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge the value of justice and injustice, imagine two extreme lives: one entirely unjust yet reputed just, and one entirely just yet reputed unjust — then compare their happiness to test whether justice is intrinsically good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device isolates variables (reputation vs reality) and demands accounting for effects of justice/injustice on the possessor, seen or unseen, as the standard of moral evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of conventional piety and prophetic/poetic assurances
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular religion and poetry are accused of portraying justice/virtue as instruments for gaining divine favor (material blessings, long posterity) or for avoiding underworld punishments via rituals; these portrayals encourage appearances-over-substance morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates and interlocutors treat such conventional assurances as insufficient grounds for affirming justice's intrinsic value and urge inquiry into the true effect of justice on the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of nature-appropriate occupation (do one thing well)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person performs best when devoted to the single art for which his nature is fitted; multiple occupations degrade quality and timeliness of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule supports institutional specialization in the city (including for guardians) and underlies the broader political/economic organization proposed.
